source_text: Ἄγε δή, καθάρας σεαυτὸν ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν προκατεχόντων σου τὴν διάνοιαν λογισμῶν καὶ τὴν ἀπατῶσάν σε συνήθειαν ἀποσκευασάμενος καὶ γενόμενος ὥσπερ ἐξ ἀρχῆς καινὸς ἄνθρωπος, ὡς ἂν καὶ λόγου καινοῦ, καθάπερ καὶ αὐτὸς ὡμολόγησας, ἀκροατὴς ἐσόμενος: ἴδε μὴ μόνον τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῇ φρονήσει, τίνος ὑποστάσεως ἢ τίνος εἴδους τυγχάνουσιν, οὓς ἐρεῖτε καὶ νομίζετε θεούς. οὐχ ὁ μέν τις λίθος ἐστίν, ὅμοιος τῷ πατουμένῳ, ὁ δ’ ἐστὶ χαλκός, οὐ κρείσσων τῶν εἰς τὴν χρῆσιν ἡμῖν κεχαλκευμένων σκευῶν, ὁ δὲ ξύλον, ἤδη καὶ σεσηπός, ὁ δὲ ἄργυρος, χρῄζων ἀνθρώπου τοῦ φυλάξαντος, ἵνα μὴ κλαπῇ, ὁ δὲ σίδηρος, ὑπὸ ἰοῦ διεφθαρμένος, ὁ δὲ ὄστρακον, οὐδὲν τοῦ κατεσκευασμένου πρὸς τὴν ἀτιμοτάτην ὑπηρεσίαν εὐπρεπέστερον; οὐ φθαρτῆς ὕλης ταῦτα πάντα; οὐχ ὑπὸ σιδήρου καὶ πυρὸς κεχαλκευμένα; οὐχ ὃ μὲν αὐτῶν λιθοξόος, ὃ δὲ χαλκεύς, ὃ δὲ ἀργυροκόπος, ὃ δὲ κεραμεὺς ἔπλασεν; οὐ πρὶν ἢ ταῖς τέχναις τούτων εἰς τὴν μορφὴν τούτων ἐκτυπωθῆναι, ἦν ἕκαστον αὐτῶν ἑκάστῳ, ἔτι καὶ νῦν, μεταμεμορφωμένον; οὐ τὰ νῦν ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς ὕλης ὄντα σκεύη γένοιτ̓ ἄν, εἰ τύχοι τῶν αὐτῶν τεχνιτῶν, ὅμοια τοιούτοις; οὐ ταῦτα πάλιν, τὰ νῦν ὑφ̓ ὑμῶν προσκυνούμενα, δύναιτ̓ ἂν ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων σκεύη ὅμοια γενέσθαι τοῖς λοιποῖς; οὐ κωφὰ πάντα; οὐ τυφλά; οὐκ ἄψυχα; οὐκ ἀναίσθητα; οὐκ ἀκίνητα; οὐ πάντα σηπόμενα; οὐ πάντα φθειρόμενα; ταῦτα θεοὺς καλεῖτε; τούτοις δουλεύετε; τούτοις προσκυνεῖτε, τέλεον δ’ αὐτοῖς ἐξομοιοῦσθε. διὰ τοῦτο μισεῖτε Χριστιανούς, ὅτι τούτους οὐχ ἡγοῦνται θεούς; ὑμεῖς γὰρ αἰνεῖν νομίζοντες καὶ οἰόμενοι, οὐ πολὺ πλέον αὐτῶν καταφρονεῖτε; οὐ πολὺ μᾶλλον αὐτοὺς χλευάζετε καὶ ὑβρίζετε, τοὺς μὲν λιθίνους καὶ ὀστρακίνους σέβοντες ἀφυλάκτους, τοὺς δὲ ἀργυρέους καὶ χρυσοῦς ἐγκλείοντες ταῖς νυξὶ καὶ ταῖς ἡμέραις φύλακας παρακαθιστάντες, ἵνα μὴ κλαπῶσιν; αἷς δὲ δοκεῖτε τιμαῖς προσφέρειν, εἰ μὲν αἰσθάνονται, κολάζετε μᾶλλον αὐτούς: εἰ δὲ ἀναισθητοῦσιν, ἐλέγχοντες αἵματι καὶ κνίσαις αὐτοὺς θρησκεύετε. ταῦθ̓ ὑμῶν τις ὑπομεινάτω, ταῦτα ἀνασχέσθω τις ἑαυτῷ γενέσθαι. ἀλλὰ ἄνθρωπος μὲν οὐδὲ εἷς ταύτης τῆς κολάσεως ἑκὼν ἀνέξεται, αἴσθησιν γὰρ ἔχει καὶ λογισμόν: ὁ δὲ λίθος ἀνέχεται, ἀναισθητεῖ γάρ. οὐκ οὖν τὴν αἴσθησιν αὐτοῦ ἐλέγχετε; περὶ μὲν οὖν τοῦ μὴ δεδουλῶσθαι Χριστιανοὺς τοιούτοις θεοῖς πολλὰ μὲν ἂν καὶ ἄλλα εἰπεῖν ἔχοιμι: εἰ δέ τινι μὴ δοκοίη κἂν ταῦτα ἱκανά, περισσὸν ἡγοῦμαι καὶ τὸ πλείω λέγειν.
pass_a_gloss: Come now, having purified yourself from all the previous thoughts that occupy your mind and having put away the custom that deceives you, and having become as if a new person from the beginning, as if you are about to hear a new word, as you yourself have agreed, you will be a listener: see not only with your eyes, but also with your understanding, what kind of substance or what kind of form those things have, which you call and think are gods. Is not one of them a stone, similar to the one we tread on, and another one copper, not better than the copper vessels we use, and another one wood, already rotten, and another one silver, needing a person to guard it so that it may not be stolen, and another one iron, corrupted by rust, and another one pottery, not more honorable than the dishonorable service for which it was made? Are not all these things made of perishable material? Were they not made by iron and fire? Was not one of them made by a stonemason, another by a copper smith, another by a silversmith, another by a potter? Did not each of them exist before they were shaped into their present form, and even now they can be remade? Could not the vessels that exist now, made from the same material, become similar to these, if they happen to have the same craftsmen? Could not these things, which you now worship, be made by people into vessels similar to the others? Are they not all deaf? Are they not all blind? Are they not all lifeless? Are they not all insensitive? Are they not all immovable? Are they not all decaying? Are they not all perishable? Do you call these things gods? Do you serve them? Do you worship them, and make yourselves like them? That is why you hate Christians, because they do not think these things are gods. For you, thinking you are praising them, do not despise them much more? Do you not mock them and insult them much more, honoring the stone and pottery ones without guarding them, and locking up the silver and gold ones, day and night, with guards sitting beside them so that they may not be stolen? The honors you think you are offering them, if they could perceive, you would be punishing them more: if they are insensitive, you are worshiping them with blood and floggings. Let someone endure these things, let someone tolerate them being done to themselves. But not even one person would willingly endure this punishment, for they have sensation and reason: the stone, however, endures, because it is insensitive. Do you not then rebuke its insensitivity? As for the fact that Christians are not enslaved to such gods, I could say many other things: but if someone does not think these things are enough, I consider it superfluous to say more.

choices.why: accusative of the thing that deceives

pass_b_english: Come now. Purify your mind from every preconception that occupies it, and strip away the habit that deceives you. Become, as it were, a brand-new person from the start, so that you will be ready to listen to a fresh word—just as you yourself have agreed to do. Look not only with your eyes, but also with your understanding. Examine what kind of substance or form these things have that you call and believe to be gods. Is one of them not a stone, no different from the one we tread underfoot? Is another not bronze, no better than the bronze vessels we use every day? Is another not wood, already rotting? Is another not silver, needing a human guard so it will not be stolen? Is another not iron, eaten away by rust? Is another not pottery, no more honorable than the most menial service for which it was made? Are not all these things made of perishable material? Were they not forged by iron and fire? Was one not shaped by a stonemason, another by a coppersmith, another by a silversmith, another by a potter? Did each of them not exist in raw form before they were crafted into their present shape, and even now could they not be remade? Could not vessels made today from the same material become just like these, if the same craftsmen worked on them? Could not these very objects you now worship be turned by human hands into vessels like all the rest? Are they not all deaf? Are they not all blind? Are they not all lifeless? Are they not all insensate? Are they not all immobile? Are they not all decaying? Are they not all perishing? And yet you call these gods? You serve them? You worship them, and you make yourselves like them? That is why you hate Christians: because they refuse to regard these things as gods. For you, who think you are honoring them, do you not actually despise them far more? Do you not mock and insult them all the more—revering the stone and clay ones without guarding them, while locking away the silver and gold ones day and night with guards posted beside them so they will not be stolen? The honors you think you offer them: if they could feel, you would be punishing them worse; if they are insensate, you are worshiping them with blood and floggings. Let someone try to endure these things, let someone tolerate having them done to themselves. But not a single human being would willingly endure such punishment, because we have sensation and reason; the stone, however, endures it, because it is insensate. So are you not actually rebuking its insensibility? As for the fact that Christians refuse to be enslaved to such gods, I could say many other things. But if these are not enough for someone, I consider it superfluous to say more.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the rhetorical structure and nuances of the Greek text. Pass A preserves the participial constructions (e.g., 'having purified yourself', 'having put away') and the conditional/interrogative nuances. Pass B provides a fluent rendering that maintains the meaning of the Greek clauses without adding or omitting arguments. All rhetorical questions and the distinction between human sensation and stone insensitivity are correctly rendered.
